awd_titl_txt: Planning: Collaborative: Food Security and Traditional Foods in Urban Spaces
awd_abstract_narration:
This planning award supports the development of a sustainable, collaborative, and participatory research program focused on urban Indigenous food systems in Alaska. As rural residents have migrated to urban centers, such as Anchorage, reliance on traditional foods has changed and food insecurity has increased. This work will lay the foundation for the first study of how migration affects urban Indigenous food security at the household and community levels in Alaska. The project is structured in three phases and involves development of partnerships with tribal organizations, local leaders, and scholars to identify priorities for urban food security research. Planned meetings will focus on assessing the role of and access to traditional foods in urban settings; how rural-to-urban migration affects food security; and how research can support urban food security.
 
Over the two-year duration of the project, the PI team will network with local leaders, food organizations, and scholars working on Indigenous food security and food sovereignty in Anchorage. Through a series of in-person and virtual meetings, network participants will use a participatory and collaborative approach to identify research and outreach priorities. These priorities will form the foundation of a future NSF proposal addressing how access, availability and use of traditional foods affects food security. Broader impacts include development of a multidisciplinary network of food security researchers and practitioners with Indigenous representation; a review article that addresses urban Indigenous food security; and experiential learning by two undergraduate researchers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The immediate goal of our urban traditional foods security planning grant was to develop a network of knowledgeable Indigenous and non-Indigenous food experts to inform urban Indigenous food security research and outreach imperatives in the largest urban community in Alaska: Anchorage. The long-term goal was to develop a sustainable, collaborative, and participatory food systems research and outreach program with Indigenous leaders, community members, and organizations in urban Alaska. We completed work in three project phases: Phase 1 Alaska Urban Food Security Network (AUFSN): establish a diverse network of 20 Indigenous and non-Indigenous leaders, organizations, and academics who work on issues related to food security and sovereignty in Anchorage, Alaska. Phase 2 AUFSN Discussions: Hold a series of group and individual meetings and discussions with the AUFSN to identify research and outreach priorities. Phase 3 Research Development: develop research based on our planning goals and activities to inform our future community-driven research and outreach proposal, centered on the self-identified needs and realities of communities and households in Anchorage.

Over the course of our project, we developed the AUFSN through attending gatherings like the Southcentral Foundation Traditional Foods Gathering or the Intertribal Agriculture annual meeting. Through these networking opportunities, 37 people, representing Southcentral Tribes or community/Tribal serving organizations, signed up to be part of the AUFSN. We led six different discussion groups reaching about 100 different discussants talking about access to traditional foods in Anchorage and related research and programming needs. Based on these discussions we formed researchable questions focused on Alaska Native desires and priorities and developed relationships that contributed to crafting research and programming. Over the course of our project, we wrote and submitted three major proposals to the National Science Foundation, Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and the National Institutes of Health. We expanded discussions and networks nationally and published a peer-reviewed journal article based on our work that included planning work in Anchorage, Alaska as well as research by colleagues with Indigenous Peoples in St. Paul, Minnesota. Co-authors included undergraduate students who were mentored and trained in related topics during this project.
